title: The Tabernacle, the Day of Atonement, and Christ's Blood
summary: The author describes the earthly tabernacle, with its Holy Place and Most Holy Place, and the Day of Atonement, when the high priest alone entered the inner room once a year with blood. That arrangement showed the way into God's presence was not yet open and could not cleanse the conscience. Christ entered the true sanctuary, heaven itself, once for all with his own blood, securing eternal redemption and becoming the mediator of a new covenant. He appeared once to take away sin and will appear a second time to bring salvation.
story: Chapter 8 said that Christ serves in a better sanctuary under a better covenant. Chapter 9 shows how, by walking through the tabernacle and the most important ritual of Israel's year, the Day of Atonement, and then showing what Christ has done by comparison. It is the heart of the letter's teaching on sacrifice. The argument will be completed in 10:1-18, where the author explains why Christ's single sacrifice makes all others unnecessary.
historical:
The tabernacle was the portable tent-sanctuary Israel built in the wilderness after the exodus (Exodus 25-31, 35-40). It had two rooms. The outer room, the Holy Place, held the lampstand, the table with the bread of the Presence, and the altar of incense. The inner room, the Most Holy Place or Holy of Holies, held the ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest containing the stone tablets of the law, over which two golden cherubim spread their wings above the lid called the mercy seat or atonement cover. A curtain separated the two rooms. Solomon's temple later followed the same plan, and so did the Second Temple rebuilt after the exile, though by then the ark had long been lost, and the inner room stood empty.

The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), described in Leviticus 16, was the one day each year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place. He first offered a bull for his own sins and those of his household, sprinkling its blood on and before the mercy seat, then a goat for the sins of the people, and he sent a second goat, the scapegoat, into the wilderness bearing the people's sins. Verses 19-21 recall a different event, the covenant ceremony at Sinai in Exodus 24:3-8, when Moses sprinkled blood on the altar and the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant". Hebrews adds details, such as water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, drawn from other purification rituals in the law.
cultural:
Blood in Israel's law stood for life (Leviticus 17:11 says the life of a creature is in the blood and that God gave it on the altar to make atonement). Offering blood meant offering a life. The ashes of a red heifer (verse 13) come from Numbers 19, where they were mixed with water to purify people who had touched a corpse; that was ritual cleanness, not moral cleansing, and the author makes that distinction explicit.

Verses 16-17 depend on a wordplay that works in Greek but not in English. The word diatheke meant covenant in the Greek Old Testament but also meant a last will and testament in everyday Greek. The author uses the second meaning for a moment: a will takes effect only when the one who made it dies. In the same way, the new covenant with its promised inheritance comes into force through Christ's death. Interpreters differ on whether verses 16-17 should be translated with will or covenant; the BSB uses will.
literary: The chapter is built on a contrast between two sanctuaries and two sacrifices. Verses 1-10 describe the earthly tabernacle and its rituals, ending with the conclusion that they were an illustration for the present time that could not perfect the conscience. Verses 11-14 describe Christ's entry into the greater tabernacle, with the letter's characteristic argument from lesser to greater: if the blood of animals brought outward purification, how much more will the blood of Christ purify the conscience. Verses 15-22 connect his death to the new covenant, using the will analogy and the Sinai covenant ceremony. Verses 23-28 summarize: Christ entered heaven itself, once, not repeatedly, and will come again. Notice the repeated words blood (eleven times in the Greek), once, and enter, and the contrast between hands-made and not hands-made.

outline.t: The earthly tabernacle and its furnishings
The Day of Atonement and its limits
Christ enters with his own blood
The mediator of a new covenant: death, will, and blood
Once for all, and a second appearing

doctrines.note: Christ is both priest and sacrifice. He "offered Himself unblemished to God" through the eternal Spirit, and his blood achieves what the blood of animals only pictured: eternal redemption and a cleansed conscience. "Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (verse 22).
Christ's death inaugurates the new covenant, as blood inaugurated the covenant at Sinai. He is its mediator, and through his death those who are called receive the promised eternal inheritance.
Human beings die once and then face judgment (verse 27). Christ bore the sins of many once, so that when he appears the second time it will be not to deal with sin but to bring salvation.
The chapter ends looking forward: Christ "will appear a second time" to those who eagerly await him, as the people waited for the high priest to come out of the sanctuary alive.

words.note: Skene, tent or tabernacle. The earthly skene was a real tent made by hands; Christ passed through the greater and more perfect skene not made by hands (verse 11). John 1:14 uses the related verb when it says the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us.

Haima, blood, which appears eleven times in this chapter. It stands for life given up in death. The author contrasts the blood of goats and calves, offered repeatedly, with Christ's own blood, offered once, which purifies the conscience.

Lutrosis, redemption, the release of a captive or slave by payment of a price. Christ's blood secured "eternal redemption" (verse 12). The word recalls the exodus, God's great act of redeeming his people from slavery.

Suneidesis, conscience, the inner awareness of guilt. The old sacrifices made the body ritually clean but could not cleanse the conscience (verse 9). Christ's blood does (verse 14), freeing believers to serve the living God rather than live under guilt.

christ: Every element of the Day of Atonement finds its fulfillment in Christ, as Hebrews reads it. He is the high priest who enters God's presence; he is the sacrifice whose blood is offered; the sanctuary he enters is heaven itself; and he goes in not once a year but once for all. The high priest went in with blood "not his own"; Christ offered himself. The people waited anxiously for the high priest to emerge; Christians wait for Christ to "appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him". The Gospels record that at his death the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), the sign that the way into God's presence, not yet disclosed under the old arrangement (verse 8), was now open.

hard.q: Verse 4 puts the altar of incense and several objects in the Most Holy Place. Doesn't that contradict the Old Testament?
hard.a:
Exodus 30:6 places the golden altar of incense in front of the curtain, in the outer room, while verse 4 says the Most Holy Place contained it. Several explanations have been offered. The Greek word here (thumiaterion) can mean either an altar of incense or a censer, and some translations, such as the King James Version, render it golden censer, referring to the vessel the high priest carried into the inner room on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12-13). Others note that the Old Testament itself connects the incense altar closely with the inner room: 1 Kings 6:22 describes the altar as belonging to the inner sanctuary, and on the Day of Atonement its incense filled the Most Holy Place. The author may be describing what belonged to the inner sanctuary in function rather than in physical location.

Similarly, the jar of manna and Aaron's staff were placed before the testimony according to Exodus 16:33-34 and Numbers 17:10, while 1 Kings 8:9 says that by Solomon's time the ark contained only the tablets. Hebrews may be following a tradition about the ark in its wilderness days, which is what it describes. The author himself signals that he is not giving a detailed account: "we cannot discuss these things in detail now" (verse 5). His concern is the meaning of the tabernacle's structure, a barrier between worshipers and God that only Christ removes.

questions: The old sacrifices could clean the body but not the conscience. What does it feel like to live with a guilty conscience, and what would it mean for it to be truly cleansed?
Christ entered God's presence on our behalf. How does that change the way you think about your access to God?
The chapter ends with Christ's return. How does the hope of his second appearing shape the way you live now?
